806.title: Bhaddiya's "what bliss"
806.hook: a former ruler, sitting under a tree, keeps sighing "ah, what bliss" (Udana 2.10)
806.howItsDone: Teachers in the Theravada tradition tell Bhaddiya's story to show the ease of a simple life in the forest, and the phrase aho sukham, ah, what bliss, is sometimes repeated in talks on letting go.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ananda's grief, when friend and teacher were gone. Your line was all directions dark. Did you stay close to someone grieving, or to your own grief? Today, a sigh of a very different kind. Day eight hundred six.

Ah, what bliss. Ah, what bliss. A monk sits at the foot of a tree in the forest, saying it over and over. Other monks overhear, and they worry. This man, Bhaddiya, used to be a ruler. They figure he's remembering the palace, the comfort, the power, and missing it all. So they go and tell the Buddha. The story is in the Udana, a collection of short teachings that close with an inspired saying. Today we find out what Bhaddiya meant.
screen: `AH, WHAT BLISS.` → `THE MONKS WORRY.` → `THEY TELL THE BUDDHA.`

segments.voice: First, the question. The Buddha sends for Bhaddiya and asks him straight out: is it true you keep saying, ah, what bliss? It's true, he says. Second, the reason. When I was a ruler, Bhaddiya says, there were guards inside my private rooms and guards outside them, guards inside the town and outside it, guards around the whole country. And even guarded like that, I lived afraid, anxious, always watching. Now I go to the forest, to the foot of a tree, to an empty hut, alone, and I'm not afraid. I'm not anxious. I live at ease, he says, with a mind like a wild deer. Third, the wild deer. A deer in the forest owns nothing. It isn't defending a border or counting its guards. It's light on its feet and needs little. That's the bliss he means: not what he gained, but what he no longer has to protect. Fourth, the misunderstanding. The other monks heard the very same words and took them for a sigh for the past. He meant the opposite. Bhaddiya was glad the past was over. Then the Buddha speaks the inspired saying that closes the story: about someone with no anger inside, gone beyond being this or that, free of fear, happy, without sorrow, whom even the gods can't see. Bhaddiya's words stand. Ah, what bliss, from a man who had every guard he could want, and was afraid.
screen: `IS IT TRUE YOU SAY IT?` · `GUARDED ON ALL SIDES, AND AFRAID.` · `A MIND LIKE A WILD DEER.` · `NOT LONGING. RELIEF.` · then, large: `AH, WHAT BLISS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find bliss in one simple thing. Look around for something small that asks nothing of you. The warmth of a mug. Light on a wall. The breath itself, arriving without being asked. Rest your attention there. Then notice what you don't have to guard right now: no message to answer, no problem to solve, at least for these minutes. If a quiet ah rises, let it. If it doesn't, that's fine too. The bell holds the time.
Bhaddiya's "what bliss". The former ruler's sigh under a tree: not longing for the palace, but glad to have nothing left to guard. Today's word.
Your line: ah, what bliss. Today, when one simple thing is good, a meal, a quiet minute, a cool breeze, say it quietly, and notice what you didn't have to guard. Day eight hundred six.

fork.setup: you're one of the monks. under a tree, a former ruler keeps sighing, ah, what bliss. what do you do?
options: assume he's happy, and leave him be.
assume he misses the palace, and tell the Buddha.
sit down and ask him what he means.
fork.reveal: the monks assume he's pining for his old life and report him. the Buddha sends for him, and the truth is the opposite: he's relieved.

trapdoor: what you thought: a man missing his old life.
what it means: Bhaddiya's bliss is relief: guarded as a ruler, he was afraid; alone in the forest, he's at ease, like a wild deer.
what a scholar hears: his words in Pali are aho sukham, repeated; the Udana closes the story with the Buddha's saying on one beyond fear whom even the gods can't see.

807.title: Rahula's verses
807.hook: the son who says he is doubly fortunate, son of the Buddha and heir to the teaching (Theragatha, Rahula)
807.howItsDone: The Vinaya traces its rule of parents' consent before a child is ordained to Rahula's story and his grandfather's grief, and communities that keep the Vinaya keep that rule with it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhaddiya sat under a tree and kept sighing, ah, what bliss. Your line was ah what bliss. Did one simple thing give you that, even for a moment? Today, a son with two inheritances. Day eight hundred seven.

Give me my inheritance. A small boy says it, walking behind a monk. In the Vinaya's telling, the Buddha has come back to his father's city, and Rahula's mother sends their son after him to ask for what a father owes. The boy follows, telling the monk he likes the shade he casts. The Buddha doesn't hand him land or gold. He asks Sariputta to ordain the boy. Much later, Rahula sings about that inheritance himself, in the Theragatha. Today, his verses.
screen: `GIVE ME MY INHERITANCE.` → `NOT LAND, NOT GOLD.` → `THE BOY SINGS LATER.`

segments.voice: First, the name. They call me Rahula the fortunate, he says, and I'm fortunate both ways. Once because I'm the Buddha's son. Once because I've come to see the teaching clearly. One inheritance by birth, one by practice, and he names both plainly. Second, what the second one asked of him. He describes himself as he was: blinded by pleasures, caught in a net, wrapped in craving, bound by carelessness, like a fish in the mouth of a trap. Being the Buddha's son, in his own telling, didn't spare him any of that. The first inheritance came free. The second he had to take up. Third, what he found. The pleasures are thrown off, he says, Mara's bond is cut, craving is pulled out root and all. He has grown cool, quenched. Fourth, go back to the boy in the road. In the Vinaya, the Buddha reflects that the inheritance the boy asked for brings trouble with it, and chooses to give him another kind, the kind nobody receives by blood. And the text doesn't end on the gift. Rahula's grandfather, King Suddhodana, comes to the Buddha in pain. He has watched a son leave, and now a grandson. He asks that no child be ordained without the parents' consent, and the Buddha agrees and makes it a rule. So the second inheritance cost someone something, and the Vinaya keeps that grief on the page. When Rahula sings doubly fortunate, the story behind the song has already shown both sides of the gift.
screen: `FORTUNATE BOTH WAYS.` · `A FISH IN THE MOUTH OF A TRAP.` · `GROWN COOL, QUENCHED.` · `A GRANDFATHER'S GRIEF, A NEW RULE.` · then, large: `DOUBLY FORTUNATE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name what you inherited. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one thing that came to you by birth: a face, a language, a habit of the hands, a family story. Just name it, without judging it. Then bring to mind one thing you inherited by choosing it: a practice, a line from a teacher, a way of working you picked up and kept. Name that too. If you pray, you can give thanks for both in your own way. If not, simply hold them side by side, the given and the taken up. The bell holds the time.
Rahula's verses. The Buddha's son, in the Theragatha, calls himself fortunate twice: by birth, and by the teaching he took up. Today's word.
Your line: doubly fortunate. Today, pass on one thing you inherited, a recipe, a story, a skill, to someone younger or newer than you. Day eight hundred seven.

what it means: Rahula calls himself fortunate twice, by birth and by the teaching, and says the second came only after craving's trap was thrown off.
what a scholar hears: the Vinaya's inheritance story ends not with the gift but with a grandfather's grief and a new rule: no child ordained without the parents' consent.

sources.ref: Vinaya, Mahavagga 1.54 (Rahula's inheritance and Suddhodana's request)

808.title: Sona's bleeding feet
808.hook: the soft-footed monk who walked until his feet bled, and learned about the lute (Theragatha, Sona Kolivisa)
808.howItsDone: The lute simile is retold in meditation teaching when a student is straining too hard or drifting too loose, and the Vinaya traces the monks' allowance of sandals to him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rahula called himself fortunate twice, by birth and by the teaching. Your line was doubly fortunate. Did you pass something on? Today, a monk who tried too hard. Day eight hundred eight.

Blood on a walking path. In the Vinaya's telling, a young man named Sona Kolivisa was raised so softly that hair grew on the soles of his feet. Then he became a monk, and he walked up and down in meditation, back and forth, until his feet split open. The text says the path looked like a place where cattle are slaughtered. He was giving it everything. And it wasn't working. Today, what the Buddha said to him, and the instrument he used to say it.
screen: `SOFT FEET, HARD PATH.` → `BLOOD ON THE WALKING PATH.` → `EVERYTHING, AND NOTHING YET.`

segments.voice: First, the thought. Alone in the grove, Sona reasons with himself: I'm one of the disciples who strive hardest, and still my mind isn't free. My family has wealth. I could go home, enjoy it, and do good with it. It's an honest thought, and the text doesn't mock it. Second, the question. The Buddha knows his mind and comes to him. He doesn't start with a teaching. He asks about Sona's old life. When you lived at home, were you skilled at the lute? Yes. When the strings were wound too tight, did it sound right, could it be played? No. When they were too slack? No. And when they were neither too tight nor too slack, but tuned to an even pitch? Then, yes. Third, the turn. Just so, the Buddha says: effort pushed too hard runs into restlessness, and effort too slack runs into laziness. So set your effort evenly, tune your faculties to each other, and take your aim from there. The answer came out of Sona's own hands. Fourth, the sandals. In the Vinaya, after Sona's mind is freed, the Buddha offers him sandals for those soft feet. Sona hesitates: people will say he gave up great wealth and now clings to footwear. He'll wear them only if every monk may. And the Buddha allows sandals for the whole order. So one man's bleeding feet became a kindness for everyone after him. The Theragatha keeps a song under his name, and behind it stands that lute.
screen: `I COULD GO HOME AND DO GOOD.` · `WERE YOU SKILLED AT THE LUTE?` · `TUNED TO AN EVEN PITCH.` · `SANDALS FOR EVERYONE.` · then, large: `NOT TOO TIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest your feet today. If you can, take your shoes off. Sit, and let your feet rest flat on the floor. Notice them: the heel, the arch, the toes, whatever they're carrying from the day. Let the breath come at its own pace, not pulled long and not held short. If you notice yourself trying hard to relax, that's a tight string. Let it slacken a little. If you drift off, that's a slack one. Come back to the soles of your feet. Somewhere between the two, there's an even note. The bell holds the time.
Sona's bleeding feet. A monk who walked until he bled, and was taught with a lute: effort tuned, neither too tight nor too slack. Today's word.
Your line: not too tight. Today, find one thing you're gripping too hard, a task, a plan, a jaw, and loosen it one notch. Day eight hundred eight.

809.title: Nanda's vanity
809.hook: the half-brother confesses he was vain and restless until he learned (Theragatha, Nanda)
809.howItsDone: In Theravada teaching, Nanda's story is told as an example of the Buddha meeting a student where he is, and his verses sit among the Theragatha's songs of the early monks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sona walked until his feet bled, and the Buddha asked him about a lute. Your line was not too tight. What did you loosen one notch? Today, a monk whose song opens with his vanity. Day eight hundred nine.

In one sutta, Nanda comes to the Buddha in pressed robes, with ointment around his eyes and a glazed, shining bowl in his hands. He's the Buddha's half-brother, son of the aunt who raised them both. The Buddha looks at him and says, in effect: this isn't fitting for someone who left home out of faith. Go live in the forest, wear robes made of rags, and stop caring about the pleasures of the senses. Later, Nanda made his own song about who he'd been. Today, how it opens.
screen: `PRESSED ROBES, A SHINING BOWL.` → `THIS ISN'T FITTING.` → `HIS OWN SONG.`

segments.voice: First, the confession. Nanda's verses in the Theragatha are short, and they open without a defense. Through careless attention, he says, I was given to adornment. I was restless and fickle, burning with desire. No excuse about youth or family. Just: I was vain. Second, the way out. Through the skillful means of the Buddha, kinsman of the sun, he says, I practiced properly and pulled my mind out of the pull of becoming. Third, what skillful means meant in his case. The Udana tells the story behind the word. Nanda wants to leave the order. He can't stop thinking of a young Sakyan woman who, as he left home, asked him to come back soon. So the Buddha takes him, the story says, to a heaven, and shows him heavenly women more beautiful than anyone he's seen. Nanda admits the woman at home no longer compares. The Buddha promises him such company if he practices. And Nanda practices, for a reward. The other monks find out and call him a hired hand, working for wages. Ashamed, he goes off alone, practices in earnest, and is freed. Then he goes to the Buddha and releases him from the promise. He no longer wants the prize. Fourth, notice what his song leaves out. No heaven, no prize, no teasing monks. Only the plain admission and the plain gratitude. The story is strange and vivid. The song is spare. A man who once dressed for an audience sings verses with nothing dressed up.
screen: `I WAS GIVEN TO ADORNMENT.` · `THROUGH SKILLFUL MEANS.` · `A HIRED HAND, WORKING FOR WAGES.` · `THE SONG LEAVES THE PRIZE OUT.` · then, large: `I WAS VAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: admit one vanity. Not out loud, and not to punish yourself. Sit comfortably, and close your eyes or lower them. Ask quietly: what do I polish so people will see it? A look, a title, a way of seeming busy, a carefully chosen photo. Let one come. Name it simply, the way Nanda did: I was vain about this. Then notice whether anything sits under it, a wish to be loved, or to feel safe. If something does, breathe with it for a moment, without needing to fix it. The bell holds the time.
Nanda's vanity. The Buddha's half-brother, who once dressed for an audience, opens his song with a plain confession. Today's word.
Your line: I was vain. Today, the next time you reach to polish something for show, a sentence, a post, a story about yourself, leave it one shade plainer. Day eight hundred nine.

810.title: Vangisa the poet
810.hook: the poet-monk who praised the Buddha in verse on the spot (Theragatha, Vangisa)
810.howItsDone: Vangisa's poems are kept in the Theragatha and in a chapter of the Samyutta named for him, and verses of praise to the Buddha, the teaching and the community are chanted in Buddhist communities to this day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nanda opened his song by admitting his vanity. Your line was I was vain. Did you leave something one shade plainer? Today, a monk whose gift was words. Day eight hundred ten.

It occurs to me, Blessed One. It occurs to me, Fortunate One. In a sutta of the Samyutta, a monk stands up in the middle of a teaching, puts his robe over one shoulder, raises his joined hands and says it, twice. Something is coming, and he can't sit on it. The Buddha answers: then let it come to you, Vangisa. And Vangisa speaks a poem of praise, right there, to the whole gathering. Today, the poet of the elders.
screen: `IT OCCURS TO ME.` → `LET IT COME TO YOU.` → `A POEM, RIGHT THERE.`

segments.voice: First, who he was before. In his verses in the Theragatha, Vangisa looks back: once, drunk on poetry, I wandered from village to village, town to town. Then I saw the Buddha, gone beyond all things, and faith arose in me. He didn't stop being a poet when he became a monk. The poetry turned toward something. Second, the danger in the gift. Another sutta in the same collection says that Vangisa, because of his own quickness with words, looked down on other monks, good and steady ones. And then he caught himself, and turned his poetry on his own pride: drop the conceit, he tells himself, it leads nowhere good. The same tongue that praised could also sneer, and he knew it. Third, the question. After one of his poems of praise, the Buddha asks him something a teacher of writing might ask. Vangisa, were these verses thought out beforehand, or did they come to you on the spot? On the spot, he says. Then, says the Buddha, let a few more come. He doesn't warn him off spontaneity. He asks for more. Fourth, what the praise is for. Vangisa's poems praise the Buddha, Sariputta, the teaching, the gathered monks. Praise, in these suttas, isn't flattery, and it isn't a performance for the poet. It's a way of seeing clearly what's good in front of you and saying so, out loud, while the person can hear it. For a man who once used words to look down on people, that's a turn worth singing about.
screen: `DRUNK ON POETRY, VILLAGE TO VILLAGE.` · `THE GIFT THAT LOOKED DOWN.` · `PLANNED, OR ON THE SPOT?` · `SAYING WHAT'S GOOD, OUT LOUD.` · then, large: `PRAISE, IN VERSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: praise someone in one line. Sit back, and give the breath a minute to slow down. Bring one person to mind, someone whose goodness you've seen up close and maybe never named. Let a single line about them form. It doesn't need to rhyme, or be clever. It only needs to be true: she stays when things get hard, or he listens like it matters. Turn the line over once or twice until it sounds right. Then rest with the line, and with the person it's about. The bell holds the time.
Vangisa the poet. A monk who once looked down on others with his gift, and learned to use it to praise what's good, on the spot. Today's word.
Your line: praise, in verse. Today, say or send your one line of praise to the person it's about, while they can hear it. Day eight hundred ten.

screen: `DAY 810 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: OLD AGE, IN THEIR WORDS.`

trapdoor: what you thought: a monk who wrote nice poems.
what it means: Vangisa's gift turned from wandering and pride to praising what's good, on the spot.
what a scholar hears: his poems are kept twice, in the Theragatha and in the Samyutta's own chapter for him, where the Buddha asks if they were planned.

811.title: Old age, in their words
811.hook: monks and nuns alike write about ageing without flinching
811.howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries, reflections on aging, sickness and death are part of the chanting, and the scenes of the Buddha's own aging body are retold when teachers speak about impermanence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vangisa the poet stood up mid-teaching and let a poem come. Your line was praise in verse. Did your one line reach the person it was about? Today, the elders and the aging body. Day eight hundred eleven.

An old man is sitting with his back to the evening sun, warming it. A younger man is rubbing his arms and legs. That's how a short sutta in the Samyutta opens, and the old man is the Buddha. The younger is Ananda, his attendant. And as he works, Ananda says what he sees, out loud, to his teacher's face. Today, how the elders talk about growing old: the nuns, the monks, and the teacher himself.
screen: `A BACK WARMED IN THE EVENING SUN.` → `ANANDA SAYS WHAT HE SEES.` → `THE ELDERS ON GROWING OLD.`

segments.voice: First, what Ananda says. It's a wonder, he tells the Buddha: your skin is no longer clear and bright, your limbs are slack and wrinkled, your body leans forward, and your senses have changed. No softening. He doesn't say you look great for your age. Second, how the Buddha answers. So it is, Ananda. Youth is subject to aging, health to sickness, life to death. He doesn't correct Ananda, and he doesn't comfort him. He agrees. Then he speaks verses that are startling from a calm teacher: shame on you, wretched old age, maker of ugliness. The verses go on to say that this lovely body is trampled down by age, and that no one escapes death. Third, the cart. In the long sutta of his last journey, the Buddha says it himself: I'm old now, worn out, near the end. Like an old cart kept going by being tied together with straps, this body is kept going. He adds that it's at ease only when he rests in a deep, quiet meditation. Fourth, the sisters said it too. Earlier in this block, Ambapali sang of her black hair gone white, her body changed, and her refrain that the truth-speaker's word holds true. Sona sang of finding strength late. Monks and nuns, the teacher and the taught, all look straight at the same thing. None of them pretend. In these texts, seeing it plainly is part of the path, not a failure of it. The body is described as it is, and the description is said kindly, to a teacher's face.
screen: `YOUR SKIN IS NO LONGER CLEAR.` · `SO IT IS, ANANDA.` · `AN OLD CART HELD WITH STRAPS.` · `THE SISTERS SAID IT TOO.` · then, large: `WITHOUT FLINCHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one honest line about aging. For now, write it in your head. Sit, and feel the body you're sitting in. Notice one place in your body that has changed: a knee, your eyes, your hands, the way you get up from a chair. Look at it the way Ananda looked: plainly, kindly. Let one sentence form, true and simple. My hands are slower than they were. Then let it sit there, without adding a complaint or a cure. After the bell, you can write it down. The bell holds the time.
Old age. In the elders' words, it's named plainly: the slack skin, the bent back, the cart held with straps, said kindly and without pretending. Today's word.
Your line: without flinching. Today, when someone older mentions their body, listen to the whole thing without rushing to reassure them. Day eight hundred eleven.

the Buddha compares his body to an old cart

only the nuns sing about aging

options: nothing: it would be unkind to mention it.
tell him plainly what you see.

fork.reveal: Ananda names it all: the skin, the limbs, the stoop, the senses. the Buddha agrees, so it is, and speaks verses about old age.

original.note: Pali jara: aging, old age. the word at the center of the Buddha's answer to Ananda.

trapdoor: what you thought: religious texts would make old age sound peaceful.
what it means: the elders and the Buddha name aging plainly, even harshly, without pretending.
what a scholar hears: the sutta's verses curse old age as a maker of ugliness, and the same teacher calls his own body an old cart held with straps.

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 48.41 (Jara Sutta: Ananda and the Buddha's aging body)
Digha Nikaya 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta 2.25 (the old cart)

812.title: Which voice is yours
812.hook: of all the elders' songs, one sounds like you
812.howItsDone: The Theragatha and Therigatha keep each poem under its singer's name, so a reader can come back to one voice at a time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ananda told his teacher plainly how old he looked, and the Buddha said, so it is. Your line was without flinching. Did you listen all the way through? Today, the week ends, and we listen back. Day eight hundred twelve.

Ah, what bliss. I was vain. Fortunate both ways. It occurs to me. So it is. Five lines from one week, and no two of them sound alike. A former ruler sighing under a tree. A half-brother confessing. A son counting his blessings. A poet who couldn't sit on a poem. An old teacher agreeing that he's old. The elders' songs aren't one voice. They're a crowd. Today, before this block of songs closes, a quiet question: which voice is yours?
screen: `FIVE LINES, FIVE VOICES.` → `NOT ONE VOICE, A CROWD.` → `WHICH ONE IS YOURS?`

segments.voice: First, the voices that confess. Nanda: I was given to adornment. Uttama, among the sisters, left her cell again and again before the day she stayed. Talaputa, the actor, argues with his own restless mind: when will it be? These songs start with the trouble and don't hide it. Second, the voices that delight. Bhaddiya, once a ruler with guards inside and outside his palace, now sits at the root of a tree, unafraid, sighing, ah, what bliss. Mahakassapa loves his rocky hills. Subhuti tells the rain to go ahead and fall. Third, the voices that grieve and turn. Ananda after the passing, every direction dark. Kisa Gotami, praising good friends, then telling her grief, then the deathless. Patacara, drawing down a lamp's wick with a needle. Fourth, the plain voices. Mutta, glad to be free of the mortar, the pestle and her crooked husband. Ambapali, her hair once black. Rahula, counting what he inherited. Sona, taught by a lute, not too tight. No one in these collections is asked to sound like anyone else. Each song keeps its singer's name and its singer's temper. The tradition kept the delighted and the mourner, the poet and the penitent, side by side. So the question isn't which voice is best. It's which one you'd recognize if you heard it across a room.
screen: `VOICES THAT CONFESS.` · `VOICES THAT DELIGHT.` · `VOICES THAT GRIEVE AND TURN.` · `PLAIN VOICES.` · then, large: `WHICH VOICE IS YOURS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reread the poem most like you. Sit quietly. Let the singers pass by, one at a time: the confessor, the one in the hills, the mourner, the plain speaker. Don't choose the one you'd like to be. Notice the one you already sound like on an ordinary day. Stay with that song. Recall one line of it, as close as you can. Let it repeat, slowly, in time with the breath. If two voices come, that's fine; let them take turns. After the bell, you can find the poem and read it again. The bell holds the time.
Which voice is yours. The elders' songs are a crowd of named voices, confessing, delighting, grieving, speaking plainly, each kept in its own temper. Today's word.
Your line: which voice is yours. Today, tell one person which of the elders' songs sounds most like you, and why. Day eight hundred twelve.

fork.setup: you're one of the monks keeping the elders' songs. Nanda's opens with a plain confession: I was given to adornment. what do you do with it?
options: leave it out: it doesn't flatter him.
soften it into something more dignified.
keep it as he said it, under his name.
fork.reveal: the Theragatha keeps Nanda's confession as it stands, under his name, beside songs of delight and grief.

original.note: Pali gatha: a verse. Theragatha and Therigatha are the verses of the elder monks and the elder nuns.

trapdoor: what you thought: holy poems all sound the same.
what it means: the elders' songs keep many distinct voices: confessing, delighting, grieving, plain.
what a scholar hears: each poem is kept under a named singer, so the collections read less like one teaching and more like a gathering of people.
